questions.q: A human somatic cell normally contains 46 chromosomes. If non-disjunction of chromosome 21 occurs during meiosis I in the mother, what is the chromosome composition of the resulting egg before fertilisation?
questions.a: The egg will have 24 chromosomes: two copies of chromosome 21 (n+1 = 24) instead of one. A wrong answer of "23 chromosomes with an extra chromosome 21" reveals the student does not understand that non-disjunction in meiosis I fails to separate homologous chromosomes, so both homologues of chromosome 21 go into one gamete, increasing the total chromosome count by one. A wrong answer of "22 chromosomes" reveals confusion with meiosis II non-disjunction where sister chromatids fail to separate.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why a triploid (3n) banana plant is fertile and vigorous while a human trisomy 21 (47,XX,+21) causes Down syndrome, even though both have "extra chromosomes."
questions.a: Triploid banana has three complete sets of every chromosome (balanced gene dosage across the genome), allowing relatively normal meiosis through alternative pairing, while human trisomy 21 has only one chromosome in triplicate creating severe gene dosage imbalance for hundreds of genes on chromosome 21. A wrong answer focusing only on "extra genetic material" without distinguishing whole-set vs single-chromosome imbalance reveals the student misses the core concept of genomic balance. A wrong answer claiming triploids are always sterile reveals confusion - triploid bananas are sterile (seedless) but propagated vegetatively, which is agriculturally advantageous.

questions.q: A cytogeneticist analyses a skin cell from a male patient and finds 47 chromosomes. The karyotype shows two X chromosomes and one Y chromosome. Write the standard karyotype notation for this condition and determine whether this resulted from non-disjunction in the father's meiosis I, father's meiosis II, mother's meiosis I, or mother's meiosis II.
questions.a: Karyotype: 47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome). The extra X chromosome must have come from the mother (since father contributes Y to make a male). Non-disjunction in mother's meiosis I would produce an XX egg (both homologous X chromosomes), which fertilised by Y sperm gives XXY. Non-disjunction in mother's meiosis II would produce an egg with two identical sister chromatids of one X, also giving XXY. Both are possible; karyotype alone cannot distinguish. A wrong answer of "47,XYY" reveals confusion about sex chromosome composition. A wrong answer attributing the extra X to the father reveals misunderstanding that father contributes either X or Y, not both.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the following two scenarios: (A) A tetraploid (4n) maize plant produced by colchicine treatment of a diploid (2n=20) line. (B) A human conceptus with 92 chromosomes (4n) resulting from fertilisation of a diploid egg by a diploid sperm. Analyse the expected viability and phenotypic consequences in each case.
questions.a: Scenario A: Tetraploid maize (4n=40) is viable, often larger ("gigas" effect), fertile due to even chromosome pairing (bivalents or quadrivalents), and used in agriculture. Scenario B: Human tetraploid (92,XXXX or 92,XXYY) is almost always lethal, causing early miscarriage; rare live births show severe malformations and die soon after birth. The difference stems from: (1) Plants tolerate gene dosage changes better due to flexible development and lack of sex chromosome dosage compensation, (2) Animals have strict X-inactivation and autosomal dosage sensitivity, (3) Plant meiosis can accommodate multivalents, animal meiosis cannot. A wrong answer claiming both are equally viable reveals lack of understanding of fundamental differences in developmental constraints between kingdoms.

questions.q: A research student claims: "Since polyploidy involves whole genome duplication, it should be harmless because all genes are duplicated equally, maintaining stoichiometric balance." Evaluate this claim with specific reference to why autopolyploids often show reduced fertility while allopolyploids are frequently fertile.
questions.a: The claim is partially correct but incomplete. While polyploidy maintains relative gene dosage (balance), autopolyploids (e.g., 4x from same species) form multivalents during meiosis leading to unbalanced gametes and reduced fertility. Allopolyploids (e.g., wheat, 6x from hybridisation + chromosome doubling) have divergent homologous chromosomes that pair only with their true homologues (disomic inheritance), restoring fertility. Additionally, even in allopolyploids, gene expression changes (dosage effects, epigenetic modifications) can cause phenotypic novelty. A wrong answer stating "polyploidy is always harmless" ignores meiotic complications. A wrong answer claiming "all polyploids are sterile" confuses autopolyploids with allopolyploids.

questions.q: Design a hypothetical crop improvement program using polyploidy to develop a new variety of a diploid vegetable (2n=18) with larger edible parts and seedlessness. Outline the steps, the type of polyploidy you would induce, and the cytogenetic verification methods at each stage.
questions.a: Steps: (1) Treat diploid (2n=18) meristems with colchicine to inhibit spindle formation, producing autotetraploid (4n=36) sectors. (2) Verify by root tip chromosome counting (expect 36) and pollen size measurement (larger in 4x). (3) Cross autotetraploid (4x) as female with diploid (2x) male to produce triploid (3n=27) seeds. (4) Verify triploidy by chromosome count (27) and confirm seedlessness due to meiotic irregularity. (5) Propagate triploid vegetatively for uniform crop. Cytogenetic methods: Feulgen-stained root tip squashes for chromosome counts, flow cytometry for nuclear DNA content, pollen viability staining. A poor answer omits the triploid bridge step or suggests using autotetraploid directly (which would be fertile and seeded), revealing misunderstanding that triploidy causes seedlessness via unbalanced gametes.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Numerical chromosomal ______ are deviations from the normal diploid chromosome number (2n) involving gain or loss of individual chromosomes (aneuploidy) or entire chromosome sets (polyploidy).
Fill in the blank: Imagine a farmer notices that his wheat plants have unusually large grains and ______ growth compared to wild varieties.
What is Numerical chromosomal abnormalities? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Numerical chromosomal abnormalities are deviations from the normal diploid chromosome number (2n) involving gain or loss of individual chromosomes (aneuploidy) or entire chromosome sets (polyploidy).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Numerical chromosomal abnormalities are deviations from the normal diploid chromosome number (______n) involving gain or loss of individual chromosomes (aneuploidy) or entire chromosome sets (polyploidy).
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) distinguish between aneuploidy and polyploidy using karyotype notation (e.g., 47,XX,+21 vs 69,XXX), (2) explain the mechanism of non-disjunction in meiosis I vs meiosis II and predict resulting gamete compositions, and (3) calculate the expected chromosome number in somatic cells given a specific.
